https://knpr.org/npr/2026-09-16/doj-char.text: Newsletters Newsletters On Air Now Playing News 88.9 KNPR Live On Air Now Playing Classical 89.7 KCNV Live On Air Now Playing KNPR Newscast NPR DOJ charges Russian agents with plotting attacks, including in the U.S. NPR | By Ryan Lucas Published September 16, 2026 at 10:19 AM PDT Facebook Twitter Bluesky LinkedIn Email Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche delivers remarks during a press briefing in the Rose Garden of the White House on Tuesday. The Justice Department has brought charges against five suspected Russian intelligence operatives for allegedly plotting attacks against the Kremlin's perceived enemies around the world, including the murder-for-hire of at least one prominent dissident in the U.S. The indictment, which was unsealed in federal court in Manhattan, says the defendants belong to a network that "is one arm of the Russian Federation's apparatus used to carry out external attacks, including murder, around the world." The network also allegedly conducted operations against civilian and military targets in European allies of Ukraine. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the two countries have been locked in a bloody war since then. Several European allies of Ukraine, including Poland, Germany and Czechia, have accused Russia of conducting sabotage attacks on their soil in recent years. Now, the U.S. is making similar allegations in a criminal indictment against specific, alleged Russian operatives. "It is our job to stop America's adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil," Attorney General Todd Blanche said. "And that's precisely what we are doing thanks to the work of the FBI and our Justice Department prosecutors." Court papers identify two of the defendants as Yuri Khrameev, a former colonel in the Russian intelligence service, and his son, Kirill Khrameev, who is a suspected officer in Russia's FSB intelligence agency. The other defendants are Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, both from Cuba, and Angel Eduardo Castro, who is from Venezuela. Prosecutors say all three men live in Russia. The five defendants are charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, while Yuri Khrameev, Suarez and Castro also face one count of murder-for-hire conspiracy. Officials say all of the defendants remain at large. Venezuelan alleged to seek murder of Russian dissident The indictment paints a detailed picture of the defendants' alleged efforts since 2024 to recruit and carry out a series of targeted killings and acts of sabotage on behalf of the Russian government. One of the alleged plots took place between July and August 2026, when prosecutors say the network recruited a Venezuelan citizen, identified only as U.S. Resident 1, living in Brooklyn to surveil and murder a prominent Russian dissident in the U.S. The dissident is not named in court papers. Prosecutors say Castro and Suarez used an encrypted messaging app to communicate with U.S. Resident 1, and gave him two addresses to surveil that were associated with the dissident. They also provided detailed instructions on how to take photos and videos of the locations. Suarez allegedly stated the addresses were associated with someone they "want to eliminate they want to disappear," and offered $40,000 "for whoever does the work." U.S. Resident 1 said he was willing to take photos and videos but not commit murder. The indictment says Suarez then asked U.S. Resident 1 if he knew "someone who wants to do construction," which prosecutors say was code for "carrying out the murder." Suarez allegedly stated that he was under pressure from his boss to get the job done. He also said that he had a team in Mexico who could do it but that they weren't immediately available. U.S. citizen allegedly recruited in Lithuania The indictment also chronicles a separate alleged plot in Europe in 2025 involving efforts to recruit a U.S. citizen to surveil and murder a Kremlin critic believed to be living in Vilnius, Lithuania. In late June 2025, prosecutors say, the American met with Kirill Khrameev at the Estonia-Russia border, where Khrameev offered to pay the American, who is not named, to take photos of an address in Vilnius. The American then kept in touch via an encrypted messaging app with Yuri Khrameev, who told him he needed to send photos or videos of the target's residence every two to three days, according to the indictment. Court papers say Yuri Khrameev told the American that the individual was being targeted for "spreading dirt" about Russia and "telling the media and the common people that the Russians are the aggressors." The indictment says the American was offered $25,000 to carry out the murder, which Khrameev said could be conducted by "throwing a bottle of gasoline" or "sticking a knife" in the victim, but the American declined, fearing he would easily be caught. Yuri Khrameev then offered him a "simpler job," such as setting fire to a warehouse or electrical substation, according to prosecutors. "I am interested in all the countries that are helping Ukraine," Khrameev allegedly wrote the American, adding that he was interested in targeting "military facilities and dual-use facilities… located in the countries of the NATO military bloc." "Serious money for serious work" "I'm offering serious money for serious work," he allegedly added. The indictment appears to include details related to some other countries' allegations of Russian sabotage. It says that Durruthy, one of the Cubans, played a role in coordinating travel and payment for terrorist acts, including in Prague. The indictment says he transferred more than $1,000 in cryptocurrency to a "criminal associate" and booked hotels in the Czech Republic and in Poland for the associate. The indictment includes a photo pulled from an online account associated with Durruthy that prosecutors say appears to show potential attack sites in the Polish capital. https://www.dw.com/en/thousands-of-germa.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OHFE Online gambling is considered highly addictive because of the anonymity of the players and the 24-7 availability among other factors Image: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement A German court has followed the European Court of Justice in finding that gamblers can seek compensation from gambling companies if they lost money when online casinos and fruit machines were illegal in Germany . The verdicts could have major consequences for gambling addicts , as thousands of people could potentially bring civil lawsuits against gambling companies. A series of court decisions at regional, federal, and European level have found in favor of gamblers in the last year, beginning with the Higher Regional Court Stuttgart in September 2025, which agreed with a plaintiff in the state of Baden-Württemberg who sued the Malta-based online betting company Tipico Games. The plaintiff lost around €10,000 ($11,200) between 2020 and 2022, but because online gambling was prohibited in Germany until 2021, the court found that operators had therefore received the winnings without legal basis and must return them. Wins for the losers Tipico Games then appealed to the Federal Court of Justice (BGH), the highest civil and criminal court in Germany. In an initial verbal hearing in mid-September this year, the court followed the principle of the plaintiffs' case on one key point: That gamblers have the right to claim back losses if the companies did not have a license in Germany at the time the losses were incurred. But a final decision on the case is only expected to be made in January 2027. Online casinos and fruit machines were banned in Germany from 2008 to 2021, but several gambling operators were active in the country because they had gaming licenses in other EU countries. What online gambling companies don't want you to know To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In April this year, the European Court of Justice ruled that EU law does not preclude a member state from "prohibiting certain services," or from "attaching civil-law consequences to that prohibition." In other words, even if a gambling company has a legitimate license in one member state, that doesn't override national gambling laws elsewhere. Thomas Dünchheim, a business lawyer at global law firm Greenberg Traurig who specializes in gambling law, said law firms were now gathering clients — sometimes trawling the internet with the help of AI tools — to prepare massive collective lawsuits. Dünchheim himself has people who have lost tens of thousands of euros come to him seeking representation. "The pendulum is swinging more and more towards the consumer. It's a bit like in America — we're seeing a mass phenomenon like the Dieselgate lawsuits against VW ," he told DW. "And there are lawyers who will collect all these little cases, bundle them, and then maybe even drive it forward with the help of a legal financing firm. It's a good business for all involved, and the ones that will have to pay are the gambling firms who operated unlawful gambling in Germany." The dangers of online gambling The decisions could bring a measure of help for addicts, as online gambling can be particularly dangerous for people with addiction issues. According to Tobias Hayer, a psychologist at the Institute for Public Health and Nursing Research at Bremen University, that comes down to four main features of online gambling: Anonymity and the consequent lack of social control, 24/7 accessibility, the frictionless nature of cashless transactions, and the high frequency of games played. "These court verdicts are not surprising at all," Hayer told DW, but he added that he had an ambivalent attitude to them. "On the one hand I can imagine that this will be a huge relief to many gamblers who had an addiction problem. On the other hand, if these people suddenly get a lot of money in their hands, but they haven't worked through their problems, then of course there's a danger of recidivism." Hooked on Gambling To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The legal obstacles But Dünchheim suggested that the gamblers may not have such an easy ride when making their claims. It's true that German law has now concluded that if the gambling contract that the player makes with the company turns out to be unlawful in the country where they live, the player can claim their losses back. But only if the player themselves "did not act illegally," as Dünchheim put it. "You also have to say: Many of these players deliberately went to games in this gray zone because the winnings are potentially bigger," he said. "Because the companies don't pay taxes." "Then the defense team of the gambling company will of course say: 'You took part in an illegal game yourself, so you were acting illegally.' And this question of interpretation is not simple," he added. "It's a very interesting intellectual question, but it's also existential for the gambling companies." Tipico's gambling gray zone The Tipico case is perhaps particularly interesting in the German context because, although the company is based in Malta, it was founded in 2004 by a group of German lawyers. The company is a big employer, with several thousand employees worldwide, and has been a sponsor of more than one top German football club. Tipico has also said that it has rigorous consumer protection measures in place to identify and prevent dangerous betting behavior. But there was some legal ambiguity about its online operations in Germany up until 2021. "They always had lawyers who could attest that what they are doing conforms to European law, because it is permitted in a European Union member state," said Dünchheim. "But that is a false assumption, as it has now been established that a gambling permit in another EU state doesn't apply in Germany, because unlike other areas, gambling law isn't harmonized across the bloc." "Tipico was started by two businessmen and grew big in a gray zone," as Dünchheim put it. "They had professional lobbying firms on board and they hired experienced lawyers, they had private equity firms on board. But of course they are carrying a huge financial risk." Picture: Dariusz Borowicz/Agencja Wyborcza.pl via REUTERS By Alan Charlish Three people were injured in a stabbing attack at a further education college in Warsaw on Saturday, police said, the latest in a series of incidents that have stoked concerns in Poland about copycat violence among young people. On Friday thousands of police visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after two stabbing sprees by teenagers in as many days sparked rumours of potential further attacks, fears that Saturday’s incident is likely to intensify. “At 12:30 today, we received a report of an incident involving the use of a dangerous weapon,” police spokesperson Jakub Filipiak told Reuters. “One person was injured and transported to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. Two other bystanders also sustained injuries but did not require hospitalisation.” He said the attacker was a 21-year-old student of the college. State news agency PAP reported that the victims were two 17-year-old girls and a 24-year-old woman who had come to submit enrolment documents. Preliminary police findings indicated the attacker and victims did not know one other, PAP reported. Police said on Saturday they had inspected some 50,000 facilities since Friday and detained 76 people. Authorities had previously said most of the people detained were teenagers who had made threats online. On Thursday, a 15-year-old former pupil wearing a helmet-mounted camera killed a caretaker and injured two teachers at a primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old wounded 10 people including himself at a school in Ostroleka, north of the capital. Reuters Would you like to comment on this article?
